item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton threshold applies “by a single vessel,” allowing an operator to divide recovery among multiple vessels and extract a much larger aggregate amount without meeting the definition.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Sub-threshold mining remains lawful.** Each vessel may apparently recover up to 10,000 metric tons every year indefinitely, even if the activity is plainly commercial and environmentally damaging.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Unclear annual accounting period.** “Per year” does not specify calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or a rolling 12-month period, inviting manipulation and making violations difficult to establish.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — Threshold creates timing and proof problems.** It is unclear whether all recovery becomes unlawful once a vessel passes 10,000 tons, only the excess is unlawful, or liability begins only on the day the threshold is crossed. Operators could also stop just below the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth boundary loophole.** Mining at exactly 200 meters is excluded because the definition requires depths “greater than 200 meters.”

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth is not measured or defined.** The bill does not say whether depth is measured from sea level, the water surface, or another datum, or how variable seabed depths within an operation are treated.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is too narrow and undefined.** Companies could argue that prospecting, excavation, dredging, disaggregation, pumping, lifting tests, stockpiling, processing, or collection short of completed “recovery” is outside the prohibition.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — No geographic definition of “deep seabed.”** The definition relies only on a 200-meter depth and does not address internal waters, territorial seas, exclusive economic zones, continental shelves, or areas beyond national jurisdiction. This creates uncertainty about the bill’s reach and may unintentionally cover—or omit—activities Congress meant to treat differently.

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Other mineral resources” is undefined.** The phrase could generate disputes over whether crusts, sulfides, sediments, dissolved minerals, hydrocarbons, or particular materials qualify.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — Undefined “Secretary.”** The Act never identifies which Cabinet secretary has this authority; section 6 expressly refers to the Secretary of State, making the unqualified term especially ambiguous.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unbounded and procedurally incomplete designation authority.** “Risks … comparable” supplies no factors, evidentiary standard, required findings, rulemaking procedure, notice, or effective date. That vagueness is particularly problematic because a Secretary’s determination would define conduct carrying criminal penalties.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — No mandatory backstop.** The Secretary merely may determine that another activity presents comparable risks; absent a determination, equally destructive activities outside subparagraph (A) remain lawful.

13. **Section 2(2) — “U.S. person” omits important entities and individuals.** It excludes U.S. nationals who are not citizens, partnerships, LLCs that are not treated as corporations, trusts, associations, federal corporations, and corporations organized under District of Columbia, territorial, tribal, or foreign law.

14. **Section 2(2) — Foreign-incorporation loophole.** A U.S.-owned mining company could organize a foreign subsidiary to conduct the mining, while U.S. parents, investors, officers, or contractors contend that they do not themselves “engage” in it.

15. **Section 2(3) — Covered-vessel threshold is easily evaded.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less are outside the registry, regardless of how much they recover, and operators can use fleets of smaller vessels.

16. **Section 2(3) — “Equipped for recovery” is uncertain.** Modular or multipurpose vessels could remove equipment before inspection or characterize themselves as survey, lifting, transport, or support vessels. “Gross tons” also should identify the applicable tonnage-measurement system.

17. **Section 3(a) — “Person” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the term includes corporations, partnerships, associations, governments, officers, agents, and other legal entities, even though “U.S. person” supplies only a partial definition.

18. **Section 3(a) — “In the United States” is undefined.** The phrase does not specify whether it includes U.S. territories, possessions, territorial waters, the EEZ, the outer continental shelf, U.S.-flagged vessels, or conduct directed from a U.S. office.

19. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is too ambiguous.** The bill does not say whether financing, insuring, sponsoring, contracting for, directing, processing, transporting, purchasing, or knowingly providing equipment or services for prohibited mining is covered. Companies could structure operations so the actual recovery is performed by a nominally independent foreign entity.

20. **Section 3(a) — No anti-evasion or attribution rule.** The prohibition does not aggregate affiliated entities or vessels, address beneficial ownership or control, or impose liability for causing, conspiring, attempting, aiding, or abetting a violation.

21. **Section 3(b) — Grandfather clause defeats the prohibition.** It allows “mining” under an exploration license, even though exploration licenses ordinarily would not be expected to authorize commercial extraction. Thus a pre-enactment exploration license could become a shield for full-scale commercial mining.

22. **Section 3(b) — License source and scope are unspecified.** The exception does not say that the license must have been issued by the United States, identify a lawful issuing authority, require the mining to stay within the license’s original terms, or exclude sham foreign licenses.

23. **Section 3(b) — Grandfathering has no limits or safeguards.** There is no expiration date, production ceiling, environmental condition, geographic limitation, nontransferability rule, or prohibition on renewal, modification, assignment, or expansion of a qualifying license.

24. **Section 3(c) — Environmental-assessment exception is subjective and unlimited.** An operator can characterize mining or large-scale extraction trials as being “for the purpose” of environmental assessment, with no independent approval, necessity standard, tonnage cap, duration limit, protocol, or publication requirement.

25. **Section 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activities can exploit the exception.** The text does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, prohibit sale of recovered minerals, or prevent a nominal research partner from shielding an otherwise commercial operation.

26. **Section 4(a) — Registration timing and content are absent.** The bill does not say when registration must occur, what information must be supplied, whether registrations expire, or whether changes in ownership, flag, equipment, or operations must be reported.

27. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Owner, charterer, manager, lessee, and actual controller may each deny being the operator, particularly where vessel ownership and mining operations are divided among affiliates.

28. **Section 4 — Registry obligations are effectively unenforceable.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register or file reports carries no stated civil or criminal penalty and does not itself make vessel operation unlawful.

29. **Section 4(b) — Reporting requirement is too vague.** “Describing” recovery activities imposes no required data fields, tonnage methodology, locations, dates, minerals, equipment, environmental effects, or supporting records. Certification has little value because no certification standard, records-retention duty, audit authority, or false-certification consequence is provided.

30. **Section 4 — Registry coverage does not match prohibited activity.** Registration applies only to “covered vessels,” while section 3 may prohibit operations using smaller or differently equipped vessels; conversely, registration does not itself limit or authorize activity. The registry therefore cannot reliably identify all regulated mining.

31. **Section 4 — No transparency or interagency provisions.** The bill does not require the registry and reports to be public or shared with enforcement agencies, nor does it address treatment of confidentiality claims.

32. **Sections 3–5 — No administering or enforcement authority.** The Act does not identify an agency responsible for regulations, investigations, inspections, subpoenas, monitoring, penalty assessment, or referral of cases.

33. **Section 5(a) — Civil-penalty procedure is missing.** The text does not say who assesses or collects the penalty, whether proceedings are administrative or judicial, what standard of proof applies, what notice and hearing are required, or where an action may be brought.

34. **Section 5(a) — Penalty calculation is incomplete.** A maximum of $1 million “for each day” does not specify whether penalties also accrue per vessel, operation, violator, or statutory requirement, and supplies no minimum penalty or mandatory factors. A profitable operator could treat a discretionary maximum as a cost of doing business.

35. **Section 5 — No operational remedies.** The bill provides no express authority for injunctions, cease-and-desist orders, vessel detention, permit revocation, forfeiture, mineral seizure, remediation, restoration, disgorgement, or recovery of enforcement and environmental-response costs.

36. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” creates a substantial criminal-enforcement hurdle.** Prosecutors may have to prove that a defendant knew its conduct was unlawful, an especially difficult showing given the bill’s ambiguous definitions and exceptions.

37. **Section 5(b) — Criminal fine is indeterminate for policy purposes.** “Fined under title 18” leaves the operative amount to general criminal-fine provisions rather than setting a mining-specific fine tied to profits, environmental injury, tonnage, or restoration costs.

38. **Sections 5 and 8 — Effective-date inconsistency.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, but section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. The text should clearly state that substantive duties and penalties begin on the same date and address conduct spanning that date.

39. **Section 6 — Negotiation duty is too weak to enforce.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires no successful agreement, negotiating milestones, consultation, reporting to Congress, or consequence for inaction.

40. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” could reproduce the bill’s loopholes.** Requiring prohibitions equivalent to section 3 could permit the same vessel threshold, license grandfathering, and environmental-assessment exception, rather than requiring a comprehensive international ban.

41. **Section 7(a) — Termination standard is vague.** “Without serious harm” does not define harm, acceptable risk, affected ecosystems, geographic or temporal scale, burden of proof, or treatment of uncertainty and cumulative effects.

42. **Section 7(a) — National Academies report process is unspecified.** No one is directed to request the report; there are no requirements for its scope, date, independence, peer review, public participation, or conclusions. “Acting on” the report likewise does not require Congress’s finding to be consistent with the report.

43. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution mechanism is incomplete.** The bill supplies no required text, introduction procedure, committee procedure, expedited consideration, or express presentment requirement for the contemplated joint resolution, inviting disputes about what enactment is sufficient to end the prohibition.

44. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — The sunset overrides the safety condition.** Even if Congress never finds mining safe, the entire Act automatically expires after ten years. This makes the purported precautionary prohibition temporary and gives industry a fixed date on which mining and all reporting duties may resume.

45. **Section 7(b) — Sunset may disrupt pending enforcement.** Because the entire Act “shall cease to have effect,” defendants may argue that pending civil cases, uncollected penalties, reporting obligations, or other liabilities disappear at sunset. A savings clause should preserve liabilities and proceedings arising before expiration.

46. **Act-wide — No recordkeeping, inspection, or monitoring regime.** The government has no express right to inspect vessels or facilities, require production records, use tracking or remote-sensing information, sample cargo, or verify reported tonnage and location, making the threshold-based prohibition difficult to prove.

47. **Act-wide — No citizen-suit or judicial-review provisions.** The bill offers no mechanism for affected parties to compel agency performance or challenge unlawful exemptions or determinations, and it does not specify review of Secretary decisions under section 2(1)(B).

48. **Act-wide — No whistleblower or anti-retaliation protection.** Crew members and employees may possess the best evidence of concealed recovery and falsified reports, but the Act provides no reporting channel, protection, or incentive.

49. **Act-wide — No coordination with existing licenses and authorities.** Apart from the sweeping grandfather clause, the bill does not revoke, suspend, or restrict existing federal authorizations, require agencies to deny inconsistent approvals, or clarify how conflicts with other seabed-mining statutes are resolved.

50. **Act-wide — No severability clause.** If a court invalidates a central provision—particularly the Secretary’s open-ended designation authority or an application of the prohibition—the absence of a severability instruction increases the risk that additional portions of the Act could be challenged along with it.
